title: Amino acids, proteins, enzymes and DNA; Giant covalent structures
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR25a#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR25b#t3 term and clue written for the game; BD05#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR25b#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD05#N.7, OR25a#N.4, OR25b#N.14a, BD05#N.11b, OR25a#N.14c.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Glycine
items.clue: The amino acid in which R = H: H₂NCH₂COOH.

items.label: Substrate
items.clue: The reacting molecule that binds in the pocket of the protein.

items.label: Fullerenes
items.clue: Closed cages of C atoms, such as C₆₀, that exist as separate molecules.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: Small 3-D pocket left by the folded chain, with several binding points.

questions.stem: Substance X melts at 1710 °C. It does not conduct electricity, either as a solid or when molten. It does not dissolve in water or in hexane. Which structure does X have?

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
A network of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout
A lattice of metal cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Separate small molecules with very strong forces between them

questions.explanation: The very high melting point means strong bonds break. No conduction even when molten means no ions and no delocalised electrons. Insoluble everywhere: a covalent network.

questions.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, is added to excess dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. Which species of glycine is present?

options.text: H₂NCH₂COOH₂⁺
⁺H₃NCH₂COOH
H₂NCH₂COO⁻
⁺H₃NCH₂COCl

questions.explanation: The –NH₂ base group accepts H⁺ from the acid. The –COOH stays un-ionised in excess acid.

questions.stem: An enzyme from the small intestine works best near pH 7. At pH 2 it stops working, although no covalent bonds in it break. Which explanation is best? (Hint: some side chains end in –COO⁻ at pH 7.)

options.text: H⁺ turns –COO⁻ side chains into –COOH; ionic attractions are lost and the active site changes shape.
The acid rapidly hydrolyses the peptide links, so the enzyme breaks apart into its separate amino acids.
H⁺ ions occupy the active site and are held there in place of the substrate molecules.
At pH 2 the substrate molecules move more slowly, so fewer of them collide with the enzyme.

questions.stem: Silicon carbide, SiC, is a covalent network solid. Every Si atom is bonded to four C atoms, and every C atom to four Si atoms, tetrahedrally, in three dimensions. Which pair of properties does this structure predict?

options.text: High melting point, but soft, because layers of atoms slide over one another easily.
Low melting point and soft, because weak intermolecular forces hold SiC molecules together.
High melting point and very hard, because strong covalent bonds at fixed angles run in 3D.
High melting point and malleable, because its atoms can rearrange without bonds breaking.

questions.stem: In a folded protein, a side chain ending in –COOH and a side chain ending in –NH₂ sit next to each other. At the pH inside a cell, the first is –COO⁻ and the second is –NH₃⁺. Which statement best describes the interaction between them?

options.text: A covalent bond forms, because an acid and a base react to give a new compound.
Opposite charges attract noncovalently, helping hold the protein's shape.
Only London dispersion forces act, because both groups are in the same molecule.
A hydrogen bond forms between two H atoms, one on each side chain.

questions.explanation: The acid group has lost H⁺ and the base group gained it. The −1 and +1 groups attract: an ion–ion interaction in one molecule.
